title: How do you run an incident and the postmortem after it?
summary: Tests whether you know the shape of a real incident-response process — severity levels, a single incident commander, blameless postmortems with owned action items — not an ad hoc scramble.

slides.markdown:
"We'd fix it and move on" undersells what's actually being tested here. The interviewer wants the shape of a real incident-response process — how severity is declared, who coordinates the response, and what a blameless postmortem with concrete, owned action items actually looks like.

This question probes organizational maturity as much as technical depth: a candidate who can design a clever system but describes incident response as "everyone jumps in and fixes it" is missing a structure that matters just as much once that system is live and something breaks.

Ask whether this org already has a severity or on-call framework, or whether you're being asked to design the process itself from scratch — that changes whether you're plugging into existing conventions or proposing new ones.

Ask whether the postmortem is meant to assign fault or find systemic fixes. This isn't a rhetorical question — some organizations genuinely still run postmortems that look for who to blame, and naming the blameless alternative explicitly, rather than assuming it, shows you understand why that distinction matters for whether people report honestly at all.

Four parts: **declare severity** (so response scales to how bad this actually is), **assign a single incident commander** to coordinate — not necessarily to fix it hands-on — **mitigate first, root-cause later** (restore service before you fully understand why it broke), then run a **blameless postmortem** with concrete, owned action items.

The ordering matters: mitigation comes before root-causing, and the postmortem — with its action items — comes after the incident is actually resolved, not during it. Trying to do full root-cause analysis while users are still impacted is a common mistake this skeleton is built to prevent.

A Sev1 incident channel spins up automatically the moment the paging alert fires. A designated **incident commander** is assigned whose job is coordinating responders and communicating status to stakeholders — explicitly *not* being the one hands-on-keyboard trying to fix it themselves.

Separating those two roles is deliberate: the person best positioned to sequence a chaotic response (who's doing what, in what order, what's been tried) is rarely also the person best positioned to be deep in a specific fix at the same time. Splitting them prevents both jobs from being done badly by the same overloaded person.

During a payment outage, three engineers independently try different fixes at once with no one coordinating. One engineer's rollback undoes another's in-progress mitigation, extending the outage by 20 minutes — not because any individual fix was wrong, but because nobody was sequencing them.

An incident commander would have sequenced those actions: confirm what's being tried, hold other responders from stepping on it, and only move to the next attempt once the current one has actually been evaluated. The 20 minutes lost here is entirely attributable to a missing coordination role, not to any technical mistake.

slides.sectionTitle: Walking it: what "mitigate first, root-cause later" means
slides.markdown:
![Incident mitigation, short and urgent, followed by the longer unhurried postmortem root-cause phase](assets/mitigate-then-rootcause.svg)

Restoring service — a rollback, a failover, scaling up — takes priority over fully understanding why it broke. The full root-cause investigation happens afterward, in the postmortem, deliberately off the clock of active user impact.

This ordering exists because root-causing well takes time users can't be actively suffering through — better to stop the bleeding with a plausible mitigation now and investigate carefully once the pressure is off.

slides.sectionTitle: The trade-off to name out loud
slides.markdown:
A heavyweight incident process — severity levels, a formal commander role, a structured postmortem template — is overhead you don't want applied to every minor blip.

| Incident | Right response |
|---|---|
| Sev1: payment outage, 20 minutes of full impact | Full process — commander, postmortem, tracked action items |
| 30-second error-rate blip that self-resolved | Log it, maybe a lightweight note — not the full Sev1 machinery |

Calibrate the process to severity, not apply the heaviest version indiscriminately. Running a full incident-commander-and-postmortem process on every trivial blip trains people to see the process as bureaucratic overhead rather than something that earns its keep when it actually matters.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: postmortem action items never get done
slides.markdown:
Track them as a required category of work with its own visibility — counted against the team's error budget, or given explicit roadmap slots — rather than a hopeful list sitting at the bottom of a document nobody revisits.

The underlying problem is that action items compete with feature work for the same engineering time, and without deliberate protection, feature work usually wins because it has a more visible deadline. Making action items structurally competitive with feature work — not just aspirationally important — is what actually gets them done.

slides.sectionTitle: Follow-up: an engineer is afraid to be named for pushing the bad change
slides.markdown:
This is exactly what "blameless by design" means in practice: the postmortem documents what happened and why the system *allowed* it to happen, not who to point at. The real fix is almost always a process or safeguard gap — a missing canary gate, a review step that didn't catch the issue, a runbook entry that didn't exist yet — not an individual's carelessness.

If people fear being named, they under-report or omit details in the next incident, and the organization loses the exact information postmortems exist to surface. Protecting that honesty is not a soft nicety — it's the mechanism that keeps future postmortems useful at all.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: a postmortem with no owned action items
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "We wrote up a thorough postmortem explaining exactly what went wrong — that's the deliverable."

**Why it's wrong:** a root-cause explanation with no owned, tracked follow-up guarantees the same incident recurs, because nothing about the system actually changed. A great narrative of what happened is diagnosis, not treatment.

**Correct model:** every postmortem needs concrete action items, each with a named owner and a tracked status — not a vague "we should improve monitoring" but a specific ticket someone is accountable for closing. A postmortem that only explains is half the job; see also how a [runbook](iv-writing-a-runbook) should be updated as part of that same closing-out step.

Declare severity, assign a single incident commander to coordinate (not necessarily fix), mitigate first and root-cause later, then run a blameless postmortem with concrete, owned action items. Calibrate the weight of this process to severity — a full Sev1 response for a real outage, a lighter touch for a self-resolved blip.

Track action items as real, visible work competing with feature work, not a hopeful list nobody revisits. And keep the postmortem blameless in practice, not just in name — it documents what the system allowed to happen, not who to point at, because that's what keeps future incidents honestly reported.
